Dialogue: I set out to get the music box fixed, but it’s so badly damaged that eight repair shops have already turned me away. The last shop I tried sent me here, to this old repair shop in front of me. It might be my last hope.
A faded advertisement for machinery sales, repairs, and maintenance. The blank spaces are filled with a jumble of tiny hand-drawn flowers.
That ad looks like it’s been around for years. I hope they can fix this music box.

The little shop was cluttered but fairly clean. The golden sunshine poured in at dusk, making the metal objects on the shelves gleam as if they were made of gold. Behind the counter, a white-haired old man was dozing.
I walked over and gave him a gentle tap.
Ah, sorry. At this hour, it’s hard for an old man like me to resist the temptation of a little nap. What can I do for you, my dear?
This music box… Do you think you could fix it?
Oh… Let me see. What happened to it? How did it get this badly damaged? I'll check it first. Feel free to look around.
An old music box, small and finely crafted. Its owner has clearly taken good care of it.

I’ve always loved making and collecting music boxes. I’ve repaired more than I can count, and I’ve made some with my own hands, too. I don’t have the energy for that anymore. Every now and then, I miss the ones I made that have since found their way elsewhere. I hope they’re all being well cared for.
An old harmonica, visibly covered in signs of wear from frequent use.

The harmonica is a lonely instrument, isn’t it? Its simple notes seem made for an evening spent alone. I like to sit outside the shop in the early morning or at dusk and play a tune. If you get the chance, come by and listen. You can be my audience.
The shopkeeper examined the pile of parts with great care. He couldn’t hide how much it pained him to see them like this.
You’re lucky, my dear. I may be the only one who can help you. I made this one back when I was starting out. I still remember the lovely little girl who bought it.
Do you remember her name?

Of course. She used to come in all the time. Her name was Elena. Lovely child. I taught her how to play the harmonica, too. Has something happened to her? How did her music box end up back here in this state?
She died in a car accident. Just a week ago…
Oh… How could this happen? She was only a child when I sold her this music box a few years ago. She was still so young. How could she be gone so soon…
I’m arranging her funeral. This music box seems to have meant a great deal to her. I’d like it to play for her one last time.
I’ll help you. It’ll be my way of saying goodbye to her…

Saying goodbye…That made me think of Elena’s funeral. No one had asked about it yet. She didn’t seem to have any friends or family, and I hadn’t been able to reach anyone who could come. The only people there to see her off might be the priest and me, the person arranging it.

She loved this music box so much. She loved music. And she was going to be buried in silence, deep in the earth, with a long, lonely darkness ahead of her. A sudden anger rose in me. I couldn’t quite say what it was I found so hard to accept. I just wished more people could come and keep her company for a little while.
Would you like to come and say goodbye to her? The funeral is in three days, at Shelley Cemetery.
Oh… Oh! I’ll be there! I’ll bring my harmonica, too. I taught Elena how to play, you know. She was barely taller than my waist back then….
More memories of Elena came back to the shopkeeper. He said that what first drew her into his shabby little shop was the sound of his harmonica as he sat playing in the doorway.

She had a real gift. She picked it up as soon as I showed her how, and before long she was better than I was. I always thought she could be a musician someday. But she moved away a few years ago, and I never saw her again. She used to bring her friend here all the time.
Her friend?
A girl about Elena’s age. Long, curly hair, big eyes. Her name was Annie. She played guitar beautifully. Best young guitarist I’d ever heard.
Do you know where Annie can be found?

I hardly saw Annie after Elena moved away, but she probably didn't move away. I remember Elena used to live right here in this neighborhood. If God means for those two to meet again, you’ll find Annie.
Thank you!
Now I have to find Annie. I need to find her.
